researcher_notes: Splits the former combined tax_top_wealth axis into two independent ordinal issues: tax_top (income/corporate RATE direction) and tax_wealth (state wealth tax). Citations for established candidates carried forward from positions_tax_top_wealth.json (researched 2026-05-13) with verbatim source_quotes attached. Three gaps researched fresh on 2026-05-21: (1) Steyer tax_top resolved to 3 — his entire revenue plan is split-roll commercial property tax + water's-edge loophole closure + a special 2027 election to raise corporate (commercial property) taxes + the wealth tax; NO source shows him proposing to raise the 13.3% personal income rate or the 8.84% statutory corporate rate, so he raises effective burdens structurally without statutory rate hikes (modest raise, not substantial). (2) Thurmond tax_top coded unknown/insufficient_data — every source describes only his billionaire wealth-tax support plus a working-family tax credit; no articulated income/corporate RATE position, and per instructions we do NOT infer from his wealth-tax stance. (3) Porter tax_wealth coded unknown/insufficient_data — her platform never mentions a wealth tax and no source has her explicitly opposing/declining the billionaire initiative; KQED notes 'none of the leading candidates has embraced' it but that is silence, not on-record opposition.

hilton.summary: Would replace California's 13.3% graduated top marginal income-tax rate with a flat 7.5% rate on income above $100,000 — a large cut for top earners — and eliminate the $800 minimum LLC tax. No corporate-rate increase.
hilton.source_quote: California has built the highest and most punitive state income tax system in America, with top rates reaching 13.3 percent. ... A single, simple 7.5% rate on income above $100,000. ... No state income tax on your first $100,000.

steyer.summary: Steyer's revenue plan does NOT raise the 13.3% personal income rate or the 8.84% statutory corporate rate. It is structural: closing the 'water's edge' corporate loophole, a split-roll commercial property tax, and backing a special 2027 election in his first year as governor to raise corporate (commercial property) taxes — together with the billionaire wealth tax — to raise ~$20B/year. Because he raises the effective burden on corporations and the wealthy via loopholes and property-tax reform rather than statutory rate hikes, this is a modest rate-direction increase (3), not a substantial bracket/rate raise (4).
steyer.source_quote: I am proposing closing a corporate real estate tax loophole that's existed for over 40 years. That brings in more money to the state, that is permanent, that is completely fair.
steyer.notes: GAP RESOLVED. Politico-preview (2026-02-18) confirms he'd 'back a special election to raise corporate taxes in his first year as governor' via split-roll, and would plug the water's-edge loophole. KQED/LAist/his own issues page show the $20B plan is loopholes + split-roll + wealth tax — none propose lifting the 13.3% income rate or the 8.84% corporate rate. Coded 3 (modest rate-direction increase): effective burden up on business/wealthy, but no statutory bracket or rate hike, so short of stance 4.

bianco.summary: Signature pledge to eliminate California's state income tax entirely — including the top bracket — funded by spending cuts, anti-fraud enforcement, and expanded oil drilling. No corporate-rate increase.
bianco.source_quote: You eliminate all of the fraud, you become oil independent and use that to fund government, and now we don't have to pay income taxes.

becerra.summary: Says he would raise effective tax rates on wealthy Californians whose passive (capital-gains) income is taxed below what teachers, nurses, and firefighters pay on wages. Has not endorsed a specific top-bracket or corporate-rate change; framing is directional ('they'll pay more').
becerra.source_quote: We will make sure that those who have really large wealth, if they are paying less than a teacher or a firefighter or a police officer or a nurse, that they're going to be paying more in taxes. ... All that passive income — capital gains and other types of income — is taxed far differently.

porter.summary: Centerpiece is a 'Progressive Corporate Tax' replacing the flat 8.84% corporate rate with a graduated scale topping out around 9.75% for the largest, most profitable corporations (~$8B/year), paired with eliminating state income tax under $100K. A modest corporate-rate increase on top earners, not a substantial broad raise.
porter.source_quote: As Governor, I will launch a Progressive Corporate Tax. ... Even less than a one percent increase on the most profitable businesses earning hundreds of millions in profit will generate up to $8 billion in annual revenue.

mahan.summary: Opposes broad tax increases, says 'raising taxes isn't always the answer,' and commits to not raising broad-based taxes to fix the budget. Lone exception is a narrow sectoral tax on AI companies — not a top-bracket or general corporate-rate increase. Proposes no rate cuts either, so holds current rates.
mahan.source_quote: Raising taxes isn't always the answer, Tom.

villaraigosa.summary: Would make the 13.3% top rate permanent only conditional on a spending plan, and opposes new state-level hikes ('we can't tax our way out of our problems'). Says billionaires should pay more but that it's a federal job. Proposes no cuts and no state rate increase — holds current rates.
villaraigosa.source_quote: With respect to making permanent the 13%, which is the highest upper-income tax in the United States, I think we should do it, but not unless we do a spending plan.

thurmond.summary: Thurmond's articulated tax program is the billionaire wealth tax plus a tax credit for working- and middle-class families. No source reviewed (KQED, LAist, CalMatters, KPBS, official voter guide) articulates a position on the personal income-tax RATE (13.3%) or the corporate-tax RATE (8.84%) distinct from the wealth tax. Per sourcing rules, his income/corporate RATE direction is not coded and is NOT inferred from his wealth-tax support.
thurmond.notes: GAP RESOLVED as genuine unknown. Searched KQED tax round-up, LAist, CalMatters voter guide, KPBS, and the SoS voter guide; all describe only the wealth tax + a working/middle-class tax credit. No rate-direction statement on the record.

hilton.summary: Opposes a state wealth tax; frames California as having 'a spending problem, not a revenue problem' and opposes Prop 13 changes. His plan cuts taxes rather than adding a net-worth levy.
hilton.source_quote: California has built the highest and most punitive state income tax system in America, with top rates reaching 13.3 percent.
hilton.notes: Carried forward. His entire platform is tax reduction and opposition to Prop 13 changes; a state wealth tax is antithetical to his program.

steyer.summary: Steyer — himself a billionaire — has said he would vote for the November 2026 billionaire wealth-tax initiative and frames his campaign around taxing the wealthy and corporations to fund health care, education, and care work.
steyer.source_quote: If there's an opportunity to tax wealthy people to fund health care and education, I'd vote for it all day long.
steyer.notes: Stance 5: backs the wealth tax AND pursues the most aggressive structural package in the field (split-roll + loopholes).

bianco.summary: Opposes any new state tax; his signature pledge is to eliminate the state income tax entirely. A net-worth/wealth tax is contrary to his whole platform.
bianco.source_quote: You eliminate all of the fraud, you become oil independent and use that to fund government, and now we don't have to pay income taxes.

becerra.summary: Opposes the one-time billionaire wealth-tax initiative on stability grounds — argues California needs predictable, recurring revenue rather than a one-time levy — while saying wealthy Californians should pay more (targeting passive/capital-gains income). Skeptical of the wealth-tax mechanism but wants the wealthy to pay more, so coded 2 (skeptical, no current support) rather than outright 1.
becerra.source_quote: Most of the government's revenue is income tax ... we're only taxing those who get paid by check, by salary. And all that passive income — capital gains and other types of income — is taxed far differently.

porter.summary: Porter's platform centers on a graduated corporate tax and cutting income tax under $100K; it never mentions a wealth tax. No reviewed source (her campaign site, KQED, LAist, CalMatters voter guide) records her explicitly opposing or declining the November 2026 billionaire wealth-tax initiative — KQED notes only that 'none of the leading candidates has embraced' it, which is silence rather than on-record opposition. Per sourcing rules her wealth-tax position is coded unknown, not inferred to 1-2.
porter.notes: GAP RESOLVED as genuine unknown. Porter has neither endorsed nor explicitly rejected a state wealth tax on the record; she simply has not addressed it, instead advancing a corporate-rate alternative. KQED secondary: https://www.kqed.org/news/12079441/heres-how-californias-next-governor-will-change-your-taxes

mahan.summary: Explicitly opposes the one-time billionaire wealth-tax initiative, alongside his broader commitment to not raising broad-based taxes to fix budget holes.
mahan.source_quote: [Mahan] has committed to not raising taxes to fix budget holes — including with a one-time tax on billionaires that most of his rivals are also against.

villaraigosa.summary: Opposes the billionaire wealth-tax initiative; says billionaires should pay more but that it is the federal government's job, warning that wealthy Californians 'are leaving as we speak.' Pledges to veto reckless multi-billion-dollar state tax hikes.
villaraigosa.source_quote: What I've said is billionaires should pay more than the rest of us, but the federal government should do that because at, at the end of the day, they're just leaving and they're leaving as we speak.

thurmond.summary: Thurmond is the only major Democratic candidate besides Steyer who openly supports the November 2026 one-time 5% billionaire wealth-tax initiative, framing it as the way to fund schools, health care, and food assistance, paired with a tax credit for working/middle-class families.
thurmond.source_quote: My proposal is to tax billionaires in our state and then use that revenue for our needs. And, to give a tax credit to working people, middle-class people, so they have more money in their pocket every month to pay for the rising cost of gas, groceries, and housing.
